newsitem.title: SPAIN: MOTOR RACING-MANSELL LEAVES FUTURE OPEN AFTER JORDAN TEST.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-MANSELL LEAVES FUTURE OPEN AFTER JORDAN TEST.

text.p: Nigel Mansell did 16 laps in the wet and then left the Circuit de Catalunya to travel home on Thursday, leaving behind him a trail of unanswered questions and several furrowed brows in the Jordan Grand Prix team.

The 1992 world drivers' champion, whose wholehearted attacking driving had made him one of Britain's best-loved sportsmen, said he had enjoyed himself during his two days' testing in Spain, but made no commitment about the future.

"It was a wonderful experience," he said, adding that he "could not thank Eddie (Jordan) enough for the chance to come and do this test." As he talked freely, in his familiar publicity-conscious manner, he made it obvious he was very attracted to the idea of returning to Grand Prix racing at the age of 43, but was not yet certain it was the right move.

"I have a lot of food for thought now," he said. "Over the next few days we will be considering our future. I am leaving here with a really good feeling and I know I can do this ....If you are committed, as I am, you live, breathe and eat motor sport."

Listening to him, it was difficult not to fall under the spell of believing everything hinted at would happen. The familiar Mansell enthusiasm, his speed on the track in short bursts, his outspoken views....it was as if he had never been away.

But, in the cold light of a bright autumnal Catalan day, it was also necessary to stop and remember that this man will be 44 next August, is the father of three growing children, has riches beyond the dreams of most and in his previous attempted return to Formula One lasted only two races.

On Wednesday, in dry conditions, he was four-tenths of a second slower than his 21-year-old Jordan partner, German Ralf Schumacher, after 49 laps. On Thursday, in the wet, he clocked 1:45.79 while Schumacher did 1:43.51. On both days, Mansell was the slowest of the nine cars on the track, including the Arrows driven by Brazilian Pedro Diniz.
Schumacher, an old head on young shoulders, admitted he would have been disappointed if Mansell, after so long out of the cockpit and carrying so many years, had been faster than him.

His team chief Eddie Jordan admitted he did not know if Mansell wanted to return or not. He said: "It is up to him. He was fast, that is for sure, so he still has the basic skills and speed -- but as to his desire and commitment for 17 races, that is another question only he can answer."

Mansell has promised Jordan an answer in the next few weeks and said: "I am leaving here with a really good feeling. I have enjoyed myself. My taste for it never went away. If we had been two or three-tenths quicker we would have been fourth-fastest yesterday, so I'm absolutely delighted with that."

Amid all the talk, there were so many 'ifs' and 'buts', it was unclear what Mansell, or Jordan, were seriously thinking. Both men said the test was only "a bit of fun", but for both there is an urge to turn an amusing diversion into a serious bid for success.

Jordan need to move from the top of Formula One's second division into the first, to satisfy their paymasters in sponsors Benson & Hedges and engine suppliers Peugeot -- and Mansell, whatever he has said, has unfinished business in the sport after his abrupt departure from McLaren in 1995.

In the final analysis, however, it depends on one question. Is Mansell young enough to do the job? And only one man has the answer...which he will deliver, after careful consideration, in the next few weeks.
